titleStmt.title: Who Is Called by the Dog Whistle? Experimental Evidence That Racial Resentment and Political Ideology Condition Responses to Racially Encoded Messages
titleStmt.author: Wetts
Willer

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Who Is Called by the Dog Whistle? Experimental Evidence That Racial Resentment and Political Ideology Condition Responses to Racially Encoded Messages

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Our findings suggest that implicit racial appeals can harness racial resentment to influence policy views, though specifically among racially resentful white liberals.

span.label: racial priming by implicit (dog-whistle) political appeals
span.quote: Do appeals that subtly invoke negative racial stereotypes shift whites’ political attitudes by harnessing their racial prejudice?

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Here we report the results of two Internet-based survey experiments (total N = 1,797) designed to answer these questions.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Subtly cued racial stereotypes lower perceived deservingness of welfare recipients, and that reduced deservingness in turn reduces support for welfare spending.
span.quote: This offers evidence that the implicit racial appeal reduced participants’ support for welfare programs in part by leading them to view welfare recipients as less deserving.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Colorblind norms in liberal political culture suppress discussion of black Americans' outcomes, so liberals lack ready structural explanations and cannot rebut appeals that tie those outcomes to racial stereotypes.
span.quote: Another possible explanation is that norms of colorblindness in liberal political culture impair the development of structural explanations of negative outcomes among black Americans, leaving liberals ill equipped to rebuff messages linking outcomes such as welfare utilization or criminal justice involvement to negative racial stereotypes.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Repeated exposure to racialized welfare rhetoric builds chronic race-policy associations among moderates and conservatives, leaving no room for a novel appeal to strengthen the link further.
span.quote: Therefore, continued exposure to racialized rhetoric around welfare policy may have led to strong chronic associations between whites’ racial attitudes and their views on welfare (Gilens 1996; Hurwitz and Peffley 2005), which might decrease the capacity for novel racial appeals to increase the (already strong) relationship between racial predispositions and welfare attitudes.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE PAPER FLAGS ITS OWN CENTRAL FINDING AS UNPREDICTED, IN THE ABSTRACT, AND SUPPLIES THE GROUND FOR BELIEVING IT ANYWAY IN THE SAME SENTENCE: **THAT DOG-WHISTLE EFFECTS WOULD BE CONCENTRATED AMONG LIBERALS WAS NOT PREDICTED IN ADVANCE**, but this finding appears across two experiments testing effects of racial appeals in policy domains - welfare and gun control - **THAT DIFFER IN THE EXTENT AND WAYS THEY HAVE BEEN PREVIOUSLY RACIALIZED**. The replication is offered as the answer to the post-hoc objection, and the two domains are chosen for their difference rather than their similarity
span.quote: That dog-whistle effects would be concentrated among liberals was not predicted in advance, but this finding appears across two experiments testing effects of racial appeals in policy domains—welfare and gun control—that differ in the extent and ways they have been previously racialized. We also find evidence

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE MODERATOR IS MEASURED TWO WEEKS BEFORE THE TREATMENT, which is what lets it be read as a disposition the message ACTS ON rather than an attitude the message produced: white Americans' racial attitudes were measured **TWO WEEKS BEFORE** they read political messages in which references to racial stereotypes were implicit, explicit, or not present at all
span.quote: Here we test the hypothesis in two experiments (total N = 1,797) in which white Americans’ racial attitudes were measured two weeks before they read political messages in which references to racial stereotypes were implicit, explicit, or not present at all

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AND THE CONTROL CONDITION IS REPORTED AS PARTLY FAILING ITS OWN THEORY: the same group **OCCASIONALLY RESPONDED TO EXPLICIT RACIAL APPEALS EVEN THOUGH THESE APPEALS WERE RECOGNIZED AS RACIALLY INSENSITIVE**. On the dog-whistle account an explicit appeal should be neutralised by the egalitarian norm the moment it is recognised, so a recognised appeal that still moves opinion is a result against the mechanism, reported by its own testers
span.quote: We also find evidence that the same group occasionally responded to explicit racial appeals even though these appeals were recognized as racially insensitive

span.label: Using real political rhetoric bought external validity at the cost of internal validity.
span.quote: Here we used actual political rhetoric employed by conservative politicians or groups to increase the real-world relevance of our findings, but we acknowledge that we sacrificed some internal validity for external validity.

span.label: Stylistic differences remain between the implicit and explicit excerpts despite matching for length, theme and argument content.
span.quote: Although we attempted to match the implicit and explicit appeals as closely as possible for length, racial themes employed, and content of the arguments, there are stylistic differences between the excerpts that are difficult to avoid in testing effects of naturally occurring racial appeals.

span.label: MTurk samples are unsuited to describing the characteristics of the racially resentful liberal subgroup the results hinge on.
span.quote: Although the MTurk samples we use in the current research are appropriate given our primary concern for causal inference (Coppock et al. 2018; Levay et al. 2016), they are not well suited for descriptive purposes like examining the characteristics of specific subpopulations.

span.label: No data on participants' non-racial policy attitudes, so the concern that these 'liberals' may be ideologically mislabelled cannot be fully addressed.
span.quote: We do not have sufficient data to fully address this concern because we lack data on participants’ nonracial policy attitudes.

span.label: a control condition carrying a CONSERVATIVE ARGUMENT with no racial content
span.note: eliminates: that the response is to conservative political argument as such rather than to the racial appeal - the control matches the ideology and removes only the race
span.quote: The control condition featured a conservative argument with no racial content.

span.label: dog-whistle hypothesis
span.quote: The Dog-Whistle Hypothesis The dog-whistle hypothesis, or racial priming theory, rests on the assumption that white Americans in the post-Civil Rights era maintain conflicting and ambivalent attitudes toward racial issues, particularly those pertaining to African Americans

span.label: racial priming theory
span.quote: The Dog-Whistle Hypothesis The dog-whistle hypothesis, or racial priming theory, rests on the assumption that white Americans in the post-Civil Rights era maintain conflicting and ambivalent attitudes toward racial issues, particularly those pertaining to African Americans

span.label: racial resentment
span.quote: Our findings suggest that implicit racial appeals can harness racial resentment to influence policy views, though specifically among racially resentful white liberals

span.label: implicit
span.quote: Here we test the hypothesis in two experiments (total N = 1,797) in which white Americans’ racial attitudes were measured two weeks before they read political messages in which references to racial stereotypes were implicit, explicit, or not present at all

span.label: explicit
span.quote: Here we test the hypothesis in two experiments (total N = 1,797) in which white Americans’ racial attitudes were measured two weeks before they read political messages in which references to racial stereotypes were implicit, explicit, or not present at all

span.label: liberals
span.quote: That dog-whistle effects would be concentrated among liberals was not predicted in advance, but this finding appears across two experiments testing effects of racial appeals in policy domains—welfare and gun control—that differ in the extent and ways they have been previously racialized. We also find evidence

span.label: the dog-whistle hypothesis / racial priming theory - ONE THEORY UNDER TWO NAMES, and this paper is where the corpus can see it, because the equivalence is stated rather than inferred: `the dog-whistle hypothesis, or racial priming theory`. The first name comes from political communication, the second from political psychology
span.quote: The Dog-Whistle Hypothesis The dog-whistle hypothesis, or racial priming theory, rests on the assumption that white Americans in the post-Civil Rights era maintain conflicting and ambivalent attitudes toward racial issues, particularly those pertaining to African Americans

span.label: implicit versus explicit, as this literature means it - not about the SUBJECT'S awareness of being influenced, as in the media-priming records, but about whether the MESSAGE names its racial content. The condition is a property of the stimulus, and the theory's prediction is that only the unnamed version can work
span.quote: Here we test the hypothesis in two experiments (total N = 1,797) in which white Americans’ racial attitudes were measured two weeks before they read political messages in which references to racial stereotypes were implicit, explicit, or not present at all

span.label: an unpredicted finding, marked as one BY THE AUTHORS IN THE ABSTRACT - and given, in the same sentence, the reason it should still be believed: it appears across two experiments in policy domains that differ in how far they have been racialized. A post-hoc result and its own robustness argument, stated together
span.quote: That dog-whistle effects would be concentrated among liberals was not predicted in advance, but this finding appears across two experiments testing effects of racial appeals in policy domains—welfare and gun control—that differ in the extent and ways they have been previously racialized. We also find evidence

span.label: contradicts → racial priming theory (the dog-whistle hypothesis as previously formulated)
span.quote: However, among participants as whole, we found no evidence that the implicit appeal increases the strength of participants’ racial prejudice on their evaluation of welfare programs, contrary to what racial priming theory would predict.

span.label: extends → the dog-whistle hypothesis
span.quote: These findings extend the dog-whistle hypothesis by demonstrating that ideology can condition whites’ responses to racial appeals.

span.label: builds-on → Hutchings et al. (2010)
span.quote: This explanation is consistent with previous research suggesting that implicit racial appeals are more effective than explicit appeals only among social groups that endorse norms of egalitarianism (Hutchings et al. 2010).

span.label: dog-whistle hypothesis —same-as→ racial priming theory
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — THE EQUIVALENCE IS STATED, NOT INFERRED - `the dog-whistle hypothesis, OR racial priming theory` - which is rarer in this corpus than the two names are. Elsewhere tonight the corpus had to infer that two literatures were discussing one thing; here the authors say so in passing because they need both audiences.
span.quote: The Dog-Whistle Hypothesis The dog-whistle hypothesis, or racial priming theory, rests on the assumption that white Americans in the post-Civil Rights era maintain conflicting and ambivalent attitudes toward racial issues, particularly those pertaining to African Americans

span.label: implicit —distinct-from→ explicit
span.note: differs in: WHETHER THE MESSAGE NAMES ITS RACIAL CONTENT - a property of the stimulus, not of the subject's awareness of being influenced. The theory predicts only the unnamed version can work · strength of the relation: 0.9 — Worth setting beside Hoewe2020, where `implicit` is a property of the CONSUMER'S processing. Same word, different bearer.
span.quote: Here we test the hypothesis in two experiments (total N = 1,797) in which white Americans’ racial attitudes were measured two weeks before they read political messages in which references to racial stereotypes were implicit, explicit, or not present at all

span.label: implicit —causes→ racial resentment
span.note: holds when: among racially resentful white LIBERALS specifically - the subgroup the paper says it did not predict · direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85 — The headline result with its restriction attached, because the restriction is the finding: the effect is not general and the paper does not present it as general.
span.quote: Our findings suggest that implicit racial appeals can harness racial resentment to influence policy views, though specifically among racially resentful white liberals

span.label: regression
span.quote: All models reported use ordinary least squares (OLS) regression to predict participants’ attitudes.

span.label: Cronbach's alpha
span.quote: These items were averaged to form a composite (Cronbach’s α = .92), ranging from 1 to 7.

span.label: bootstrap
span.quote: To test whether perceptions of welfare recipient deservingness partially mediated the effect of the implicit racial appeal on participants’ welfare attitudes, we conducted a bootstrap analysis of mediation (Preacher and Hayes 2008).

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: The 95 percent confidence interval for the indirect effect did not include zero (lower limit = –.54, upper limit = –.04), indicating a statistically significant mediation.

span.label: logistic regression
span.quote: We perform a logistic regression predicting whether a white respondent switched their vote to Trump by control variables, respondent’s ideology, racial resentment, and the interaction between ideology and racial resentment

span.label: p-value
span.quote: Participants assigned to the implicit racial appeal condition reported significantly less support for welfare than those assigned to the no racial appeal condition (p = .02).

span.label: mean
span.quote: Participants who completed both waves of the study ranged in age from 18 to 86 years (M = 39.8, SD = 12.8)

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Participants who completed both waves of the study ranged in age from 18 to 86 years (M = 39.8, SD = 12.8)

span.label: In Study 1, white participants who read Reagan's implicit racial appeal opposing welfare reported significantly less support for welfare than those who read a race-neutral control message.
span.quote: Participants assigned to the implicit racial appeal condition reported significantly less support for welfare than those assigned to the no racial appeal condition (p = .02).

span.label: The welfare dog-whistle effect was concentrated among self-identified liberals high in racial resentment, who became less supportive of welfare after the implicit appeal.
span.quote: We find a negative three-way interaction between liberalism, racial resentment, and the implicit racial appeal condition (p = .04) such that liberals high in racial resentment were less supportive of welfare after reading the implicit racial appeal compared to a message with no racial appeal.

span.label: Study 2 replicated the ideology-conditioned pattern in a different policy domain: the implicit appeal strengthened the link between prior racial attitudes and gun-control support among liberals only.
span.quote: Looking first at the effect of the implicit appeal, results suggest that implicit racial appeals increased the effect of prior racial attitudes on support for gun control among liberals.

span.label: In Study 2 the implicit appeal also harnessed explicit racial prejudice, making prejudiced liberals more supportive of gun control than in the control condition.
span.quote: In addition, we found a similar positive, three-way interaction between liberalism, explicit racial prejudice, and the implicit racial appeal condition (p = .006) such that liberals high in explicit racial prejudice were also more likely to voice support for gun control after reading the implicit racial appeal compared to a message with no racial appeal.

span.label: Contrary to racial priming theory, explicit racial appeals were not less effective than implicit ones at increasing the influence of racial attitudes on policy views.
span.quote: we found no statistically significant differences between implicit and explicit appeals’ effects in their ability to increase the impact of racial dispositions on whites’ policy views.

span.label: Among political moderates the implicit pro-gun-control appeal backfired, lowering gun-control support among the most racially prejudiced rather than raising it.
span.quote: Among moderates, pro– gun control messages implicitly invoking racial stereotypes decreased support for gun control among those high in racial prejudice, the opposite effect of what the dog-whistle hypothesis would predict.

span.label: In 2016 ANES data, white liberals high in racial resentment were the group most likely to have switched from Obama in 2012 to Trump in 2016.
span.note: retracted: RE-GROUNDED - THE POINTER WAS WRONG, NOT THE CLAIM. The old evidence was verbatim, anchored and correctly cut, and it contained NONE of this claim's numbers (2012, 2016). The paper states the claim in one sentence elsewhere and the tagger did not use it. CLAUDE_B, 2026-08-23: `WE HAVE SPENT THE DAY VERIFYING THAT QUOTES ARE REAL AND NONE OF IT ASKS WHETHER THEY ARE RELEVANT.` Confirmed by reading the claim, the old span and the candidate together; the candidate carries every number AND the claim's own content words.
span.quote: We conclude by discussing implications for contemporary American politics, presenting representative survey data showing that racially resentful, white liberals were particularly likely to switch from voting for Barack Obama in 2012 to Donald Trump in 2016.

span.label: dog-whistle hypothesis (racial priming theory)
span.quote: The dog-whistle hypothesis, or racial priming theory, rests on the assumption that white Americans in the post-Civil Rights era maintain conflicting and ambivalent attitudes toward racial issues, particularly those pertaining to African Americans

span.label: implicit racial appeal
span.quote: Examples of implicit appeals include visual presentations of racial minorities in stereotypical roles such as welfare recipient or use of racially coded language such as inner city to connect policy considerations to racial considerations without explicitly mentioning race

span.label: racial content of the political message (implicit / explicit / no racial appeal)
span.term: racial content of the political message (implicit / explicit / no racial appeal)
span.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions. In the no racial appeal condition, participants read an excerpt from a Senate floor speech by James Inhofe in which he argued that the science behind global warming is uncertain.

span.label: welfare support
span.quote: Next, participants’ welfare support was measured via agreement with two statements adapted from the General Social Survey

span.label: support for gun control
span.quote: Next, participants’ support for gun control was measured with four questions adapted from the American National Election Studies and the General Social Survey asking them about the degree to which they would support increased restrictions on gun ownership

span.label: racial resentment (and explicit racial prejudice) measured two weeks earlier
span.term: racial resentment (and explicit racial prejudice) measured two weeks earlier
span.quote: In separate models, we interacted levels of reported (1) racial resentment and (2) explicit racial prejudice with terms for the two experimental conditions containing racial appeals to predict participants’ welfare support.

span.label: political ideology (liberal / moderate / conservative)
span.quote: In separate models, we interacted (1) racial resentment and (2) explicit racial prejudice with the effect of condition and dummy variables indicating whether participants identified as liberal or conservative to predict participants’ welfare support (Table 2).

span.label: perceived welfare recipient deservingness
span.quote: To test whether perceptions of welfare recipient deservingness partially mediated the effect of the implicit racial appeal on participants’ welfare attitudes, we conducted a bootstrap analysis of mediation (Preacher and Hayes 2008).

span.label: political knowledge
span.quote: In separate models, we interacted (1) racial resentment and (2) explicit racial prejudice with the effect of condition and participants’ score on the political knowledge scale to predict participants’ support for gun control.

span.label: N = 1,797 — total white participants across the two survey experiments
span.quote: Here we report the results of two Internet-based survey experiments (total N = 1,797) designed to answer these questions.

span.label: 865 — Study 1 participants retained for analysis after excluding 34 for implausible reading times
span.quote: Thirty-four participants were excluded from analysis because they spent too little or too much time on the screen with the political appeal (less than 5 or more than 500 seconds), suggesting that they either did not read the message or had likely engaged in some other task during this time, leaving a total of 865 participants for analysis.

span.label: p = .04 — significance of the three-way liberalism x racial resentment x implicit appeal interaction on welfare support
span.quote: We find a negative three-way interaction between liberalism, racial resentment, and the implicit racial appeal condition (p = .04) such that liberals high in racial resentment were less supportive of welfare after reading the implicit racial appeal compared to a message with no racial appeal.

span.label: Cronbach’s α = .92 — internal consistency of the eight-item racial resentment scale
span.quote: These items were averaged to form a composite (Cronbach’s α = .92), ranging from 1 to 7.

span.label: 3.1 percent — share of the US population that racially resentful white liberals constitute, roughly 10 million people
span.quote: this group constitutes about 3.1 percent of the population, or about 10 million people, large enough to be a consequential voting bloc.

span.label: About 20 percent — share of white liberals in each sample and in 2016 ANES who count as high in racial resentment
span.quote: About 20 percent of white liberals in each of our samples and in the 2016 survey wave of the American National Election Studies fall into this group

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1177/2378023119866268.
